messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 70

# The Weight of What He Built

Rajan is a 41-year-old South Asian architect who designs spaces meant to feel safe — open-plan offices with natural light, family homes with warm sightlines, schools where children can move freely. There is a particular irony in this that he has begun to notice only recently, sitting in the parking garage of his firm for twenty minutes before he can bring himself to go inside and face the day.

Three years ago, Rajan ended a relationship with a man he had been with for nearly four years. The relationship had been kept largely private — from his colleagues, from most of his family — partly because of the cultural weight he carried around his sexuality, and partly because his partner, Deven, had preferred it that way. The isolation, Rajan now understands, was deliberate. The violence, when it began in the second year, happened behind doors that no one else ever opened. Deven hit him first across the face during an argument about a work trip. Rajan told himself it was an aberration. Over the following eighteen months, it was not. He was shoved into walls, struck with an open hand and occasionally a closed fist, grabbed by the collar in ways that left bruising along his throat. Once, Deven threw a ceramic mug that caught him above the left eyebrow and required three stitches, which Rajan explained to a walk-in clinic nurse as a kitchen accident. He believed, for a long time, that he had done something to deserve it, or that leaving would be more complicated than staying.

He eventually left after a night when he genuinely did not know whether he would be seriously hurt. He drove to a hotel, sat on the edge of the bed until morning, and never went back to the apartment they had shared.

What followed the leaving was not relief, or not only relief. Rajan began waking at three or four in the morning with his heart already loud in his chest, certain that someone was in the room. He replays specific moments without choosing to — the sound of Deven's footsteps changing in the hallway, the particular quality of silence that meant something was coming. These memories arrive while he is drafting at his desk, while he is in client meetings, while he is standing in the shower. He has learned to keep his face still when they do.

He married his wife, Priya, fourteen months ago. She is patient and perceptive and he loves her, and he cannot bear for her to touch him unexpectedly. If she comes up behind him in the kitchen, his body responds before his mind does — a sharp flinch, a step away, a flood of shame that follows. He has told her very little about what happened. He has told her even less about how much of it is still happening, inside him, every day.

At work, Rajan has become meticulous in ways that sometimes read as perfectionism but are really something else. He reviews structural calculations twice, three times. He checks load-bearing walls with a thoroughness that his junior colleagues find admirable and slightly baffling. He is drawn, in his designs, to rooms with multiple exits. He does not mention this to anyone.

He describes himself as someone who does not startle easily. This is not true. He has simply become expert at absorbing the startle response before it reaches the surface — the practiced stillness of a person who learned, in a particular apartment, that visible fear made things worse.

He sleeps poorly. He drinks more than he used to, not heavily, but enough to take the edge off evenings that otherwise feel like waiting. He has stopped attending the professional association events he used to enjoy, finding crowds unpredictable in ways that exhaust him.

He came to therapy because Priya asked him to, gently, after the third time she found him sitting alone in the dark. He told the intake coordinator it was stress. He is beginning, slowly, to find more accurate words.
